Marathon Petroleum bounced up slightly today after losing nearly 8% over the past two weeks, but the gain masks a deteriorating situation for refiners. Refining margins—the profit from turning crude into gasoline and diesel—have been squeezed as oil storage climbed to 694 million barrels while refineries run at nearly full capacity (95.7%), leaving little room to push more product out. A major industry analyst called the "epic boom in refinery-related stocks" over as of Sunday, and that assessment seems to be reflected in the stock's sharp decline.

Geopolitical shocks that would normally prop up energy prices—Iranian tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi strikes on Saudi refineries, and new U.S. sanctions on Iran—have failed to lift the stock, suggesting markets are pricing in structural headwinds rather than short-term supply disruptions. With climate talks collapsing and no meaningful policy shift toward fossil fuels, refiners face a longer-term squeeze on demand growth even if crude prices stabilize.
